question: Formal close-out pass for four markdown engine families left unassessed by the prior wide sweep (research 0008 for MarkText's MD+CriticMarkup core parser). Verify against parser SOURCE (not just docs), with primary-source citations, whether each of these four can express the deciding requirement pair: R-1 (one CriticMarkup annotation, e.g. {++add++}, opening mid-sentence in one paragraph and closing mid-sentence in a later block — crossing blank lines/headings/blockquotes — recognized as ONE first-class entity) AND R-2 (recognized in the same single pass as Markdown: no regex prepass, no second scanner, no overlay, no post-parse pairing that revises recognition decisions) on its public extension API without forking. The four families, each needing a per-engine verdict: (1) flexmark-java (vsch/flexmark-java — its extension architecture is famously deep: custom block parsers, InlineParserExtension, DelimiterProcessor, LinkRefProcessor, and it advertises source-level fidelity / lossless AST with exact source ranges; does ANY of that let an inline construct span block boundaries in-pass? examine its two-phase structure: DocumentParser block phase then InlineParserImpl per-block; check whether its 'PostProcessor' / 'ParagraphPreProcessor' hooks are post-parse passes); (2) commonmark-java (commonmark/commonmark-java — reference-style two-phase; extension surface = BlockParserFactory, InlineContentParserFactory, DelimiterProcessor, PostProcessor; verify the inline phase is per-block and PostProcessor is post-parse); (3) swift-markdown (apple/swift-markdown — wraps GitHub's cmark-gfm C library; verify parsing happens wholesale in cmark-gfm (block-then-inline, no user grammar extensions at all beyond cmark-gfm's compiled extension set) and the Swift layer is AST visitation/rewriting = post-parse only); (4) mistune (lepture/mistune, Python — regex-driven block then inline phases, plugin system registers patterns per phase; verify inline patterns are applied per-block-content and directives/plugins cannot pair across blocks in-pass). For each: parse model (phases, where block boundaries freeze), extension ceiling for cross-block inline constructs, whether any documented extension or community plugin has ever crossed a block boundary in-pass (search issues/discussions for precedent), error tolerance model, any incremental parsing support, license + maintenance state, and the R-1+R-2 verdict with cited source files/lines. Also flag any surprising harvestable asset (e.g. flexmark's source-fidelity AST design or its formatter round-trip machinery — it advertises exact-source round-tripping for its formatter; assess whether its lossless-AST representation carries design lessons for a source-authoritative engine). Deliverable: four verdicts + any harvest notes; this closes the final asterisk on the research 0008 sweep, whose universal conclusion so far is that every evaluated engine freezes block boundaries before inline recognition and offers only post-parse cross-block hooks.

verified_claims.claim: flexmark-java parses in a fixed sequence of distinct steps in which the source is first broken into Block nodes before any inline processing occurs, so block boundaries are frozen before inline recognition — custom processing hooks exist at each step but do not reorder the phases.
verified_claims.quote: Parsing proceeds in distinct steps with ability add custom processing at each step. ... Text in the source is broken up into Block nodes.

verified_claims.claim: flexmark-java's inline processing phase is scoped per block: each block only processes inline elements within its own text nodes, meaning the public inline extension points (InlineParserExtension, DelimiterProcessor, LinkRefProcessor) operate on a single block's text and cannot recognize an inline construct that opens in one block and closes in a later block in-pass — failing R-1 within the single-pass constraint.
verified_claims.quote: During inline processing each block is given the chance to process inline elements contained in its text node or nodes.

verified_claims.claim: flexmark-java's PostProcessor hooks (NodePostProcessor and DocumentPostProcessor) run after the AST is built as a final-modification pass, so any cross-block pairing implemented there is by definition a post-parse pass that revises recognition decisions — satisfying neither R-2 nor the 'no post-parse pairing' constraint.
verified_claims.quote: Post processing step is for final AST modifications. Post processors come in two varieties: node and document post processors.

verified_claims.claim: flexmark-java's DocumentParser is strictly two-phase: parse() runs a PARSE_BLOCKS phase consuming the input line-by-line via incorporateLine(), and inline parsing occurs only afterwards in finalizeAndProcess(), where the phase advances to PARSE_INLINES after finalizeBlocks() — so all block boundaries are frozen before any inline recognition begins.

Inline recognition in flexmark-java is invoked strictly per finalized block: processInlines() iterates every BlockParser individually and calls parseInlines on each one, so the inline parser never sees content spanning two blocks — no in-pass cross-block inline construct (R-1+R-2) is expressible at this layer.

flexmark's ParagraphPreProcessor hook runs after block structure is finalized but before inline parsing, and operates on one Paragraph block at a time (preProcessParagraph takes a single Paragraph) — it is a between-phases mutation of the frozen block tree, not a single-pass recognition mechanism and not cross-block.

flexmark-java's Parser.parse() first completes full document parsing via DocumentParser, and only afterwards applies PostProcessors through PostProcessorManager.processDocument — meaning PostProcessor is a post-parse pass over a finished AST, not an in-pass recognition hook, so any cross-block pairing done there revises recognition decisions after block/inline parsing has frozen (fails R-2).
verified_claims.quote: Document document = documentParser.parse(input); return postProcess(document); ... private Document postProcess(Document document) { document = PostProcessorManager.processDocument(document, postProcessorDependencies); return document; }

verified_claims.claim: The complete public extension surface of flexmark-java's Parser.Builder consists of customBlockParserFactory, customInlineParserExtensionFactory, customInlineParserFactory, customDelimiterProcessor, postProcessorFactory, paragraphPreProcessorFactory, blockPreProcessorFactory, linkRefProcessorFactory, and specialLeadInHandler — every hook attaches to either the block phase, the per-block inline phase, or post-parse; no hook exposes an inline construct that can span block boundaries during recognition.
verified_claims.quote: customBlockParserFactory(CustomBlockParserFactory blockParserFactory) ... customInlineParserExtensionFactory(InlineParserExtensionFactory inlineParserExtensionFactory) ... customDelimiterProcessor(DelimiterProcessor delimiterProcessor) ... postProcessorFactory(PostProcessorFactory postProcessorFactory) ... paragraphPreProcessorFactory(ParagraphPreProcessorFactory paragraphPreProcessorFactory) ... linkRefProcessorFactory(LinkRefProcessorFactory linkRefProcessor)

verified_claims.claim: flexmark-java's DocumentParser is constructed with the inline parser supplied via inlineParserFactory.inlineParser(...), showing the inline parser is a component invoked inside DocumentParser's parse — the inline phase operates within the block-parsing pipeline (per-block content), and even a fully custom InlineParserFactory replaces the inline parser only within that per-block invocation contract.
verified_claims.quote: DocumentParser documentParser = new DocumentParser(options, blockParserFactories, paragraphPreProcessorFactories, blockPreProcessorDependencies, inlineParserFactory.inlineParser(...));

verified_claims.claim: For a paired custom inline construct ([green]...[/green]) that conflicts with core Markdown recognition, the flexmark-java maintainer's officially recommended path is a PostProcessor that replaces nodes in the AST after parsing, not an in-pass extension — confirming PostProcessor is a post-parse hook.
verified_claims.quote: The **easiest** way to implement what you want is to use a post processor and replace the link ref nodes with custom nodes for your syntax elements.

verified_claims.claim: The maintainer explicitly states the PostProcessor approach operates on already-parsed markdown and therefore inherits recognition decisions that cannot be revised (e.g., nesting prohibitions from link-ref parsing persist), which matches the 'post-parse pairing that revises recognition' pattern excluded by requirement R-2.
verified_claims.quote: The post processor approach will have limitations since the markdown is already parsed and `[link ref [green] green [/green]]` will not parse the outer link ref since link refs within link refs are not allowed.

verified_claims.claim: flexmark-java's inline parser entry point receives a single block's content sequence (not the document), confirming inline recognition is scoped per block: the public parse method takes the block's content and the block node, and its javadoc says it parses 'content in block'. (InlineParserImpl.java lines 372-378, tag 0.32.2)

Delimiter and bracket pairing state is reset at the start of every per-block parse call, so an inline delimiter opened in one block (e.g. a {++ opener) cannot remain pending into a later block — cross-block inline pairing is structurally impossible in-pass. (lines 379-381)

All delimiter pairing is resolved and text flushed at the end of each block's inline parse — processDelimiters(null) runs per block, before the next block is inline-parsed — so recognition decisions freeze at block granularity. (lines 383-389)

InlineParserExtension.parse() hooks — flexmark's deepest custom-inline extension point — are dispatched inside parseInline() keyed on the current character of the current block's input, meaning a custom inline construct can only match text within the block being parsed; the extension API never sees a cross-block window. (lines 617-624)

The only extension hooks with wider-than-block scope are finalizeBlock (called after each block's inline parse completes) and finalizeDocument (called after the whole document is parsed) — i.e., post-parse callbacks, so any cross-block pairing on the public API must revise already-made recognition decisions, failing R-2. (lines 391-395 and 166-176)

flexmark-java's lossless-AST/source-fidelity capability originated as a retrofit onto a direct fork of commonmark-java's two-phase parser: every parser file changed in this inception commit lives under the org.commonmark.internal package (DocumentParser, InlineParserImpl, ParagraphParser, BlockContent), preserving the DocumentParser block phase / InlineParserImpl inline phase split rather than replacing the recognition model.

verified_claims.claim: The explicit design goal of flexmark's source-position work was exact reconstruction of the original source text from the AST — i.e., source fidelity is about position preservation, not about a different (cross-block-capable) inline recognition model.
verified_claims.quote: start rework of parser to have full source position information and AST that would allow rebuilding of exact original source.

verified_claims.claim: commonmark-java's inline parsing entry point operates on the content of a single block at a time: parse() takes the block's SourceLines plus the block Node and appends the recognized inline children to that one block, so inline recognition never sees text from any other block.

All inline-parser state is destroyed between blocks: every parse() call begins with reset(lines), which re-creates the scanner from the current block's lines and nulls the delimiter and bracket stacks, so an unmatched opener (e.g. a CriticMarkup '{++' recognized in one paragraph) cannot persist to pair with a closer in a later block in-pass.

Delimiter matching is resolved entirely within a single parse() invocation on one block: after the per-block scanning loop, parse() calls processDelimiters(null) to flush the whole delimiter stack before returning, leaving no cross-block pairing opportunity.

The public inline extension surface (custom InlineContentParserFactory and DelimiterProcessor instances supplied via InlineParserContext) is wired into this same per-block InlineParserImpl in its constructor, so extensions written against the public API inherit the per-block scope and cannot recognize an inline construct spanning block boundaries in-pass — capping the extension ceiling at post-parse hooks (PostProcessor) for cross-block constructs.

In commonmark-java, Parser.parse() runs DocumentParser.parse() to completion over the whole input and only then invokes postProcess(document) — so the entire block+inline parse finishes before any PostProcessor runs, making PostProcessor structurally incapable of in-pass recognition (fails R-2 for any cross-block construct built on it).

commonmark-java's postProcess() applies each registered PostProcessor sequentially to the already-completed document Node and returns the rewritten tree — i.e., cross-block pairing via PostProcessor is a post-parse AST rewrite pass that revises earlier recognition decisions, exactly the mechanism R-2 excludes.

commonmark-java's inline extension mechanism was designed so custom inline parsers are invoked only as a per-character fallback during inline parsing — they get a chance to handle a matched character before it is treated as literal text, and operate by adding Nodes and advancing the current parsing position within the inline content being parsed. This scopes custom inline parsers to the inline phase's own scan (per-block content), not to a construct that could span block boundaries.
verified_claims.quote: When we match a character during inline parsing, the last fallback is to treat it as text. Before we do that, if there are custom inline parsers, we could call each one (with some priority maybe?) and give them the opportunity to handle that. ... In a custom inline parser, it could parse the input and return/add Nodes. It could also advance the current parsing position.
